rules_text:
Rules summary All Fours is a trick-taking card game, usually played with four players in two-player partnerships, that dates from around the 17th century. There are many rules variations, but the version implemented on Board Game Area as Caribbean All Fours is meant to be an adaptation of the modern game as it is played in Trinidad and Tobago. Contents 1 Game Play 2 Scoring 3 End of Game 4 Variations Game Play The game plays as described in the "Rules of Card Games" website under the heading "All Fours in Trinidad": link , with the following differences: No misdeal: since the game software deals the cards, there is no possibility for a misdeal, no points can be scored for this scenario No revoking/reneging: for simplicity of online gameplay, playing cards illegally is not allowed, and therefore revoking is not necessary Scoring High -- 1 point This point is won by the team of the player who had the highest trump. Low -- 1 point This point is won by the team of the player who held the lowest trump that was dealt. It does not matter who wins the trick containing this trump - the point is for the original holders. Jack -- 1 or 3 points If the jack of trumps wins a trick, or is won in a trick by the partner of the holder, the team with the jacks scores 1 point. If the jack is captured in a trick won by the opponents of the holder, the team capturing the jack scores 3 points for hang jack. If the jack of trumps was not dealt, then of course neither team scores for it. Game -- 1 point This point goes to the team that wins the more valuable cards in tricks. For this purpose only, the top five cards in each suit have the following values: ace = 4, king = 3, queen = 2, jack = 1, ten = 10; other cards (2-9) have no value. Each team adds up the total value of the cards in their tricks, and whichever team has more scores the game point. If both teams have the same value of cards, no one gets the game point. End of Game The first team to score 14 points is the winner. Note that the points are scored in order, so that ties are not possible. Variations The only variation implemented at this time is the alternate trump scoring as played in Tobago (a Two scores two points when turned instead of a Six)

---

community_text:
[Rating: 3.5/10] This game clearly offended my sensibilities, but I can't recall how.  Best guess: It ran over my dog or plowed salt into my farmland.

[Rating: 3.5/10] Quick play trick taking game. We played this a lot while eating dinner. Would not want to make a night of gaming focused on this light and lucky game.

[Rating: 4/10] TRY Sept/05: eh. 6 tricks, but for 3 of 4 points, only 2 or 3 cards matter.  Frequent re-deals too, when noone is willing to bid.

[Rating: 4/10] One of my least favorite trick/bidding traditional card games, but it's a huge game with my inlaws, so I'm forced to play it from time to time. All the action is in the bidding, and all too often, your cardplay is literally pointless, as several times a game the order in which you play your cards is meaningless.

[Rating: 4/10] I'm not a huge fan of trick taking games, and this one just didn't do anything for me.  I also felt like there were just a bunch of rules tacked on.  For some reason, the jack of the same color as the trump suit is also a trump card, and for some reason jokers are better than 10's but less than jacks.  And then 2's are an automatic point you don't even have to fight for, and so on...  I dunno, just totally illogical rules that interfere with the game play for me.  I suppose you'd just get used to it over time, but I didn't enjoy it enough to bother.

[Rating: 4/10] :thumbsdown: communal cards :thumbsdown: strategically shallow :thumbsdown: tediously tactical

[Rating: 4/10] A partners trick-taking game where you can spend the entire round on auto-pilot. There's potential here but in it's current form it's pretty dull.

[Rating: 4/10] (Comments for the 6-card partnership version Setback) A simplistic traditional game. I am not a big a fan of low trick count games - which, for some reason, were terribly popular in American culture. Pitch is like a neutered version of other games I've played where you are trying to play for multiple objectives at the same time. I'd never pick this over a climbing game or pretty much any traditional European card game - too many forced/zero-thought plays.

[Rating: 5/10] It's Setback where I'm from! I've played this for years, but there are still some subtle strategy things I haven't been able to pick up, but there is a decent amount of luck still.

[Rating: 5/10] My favorite traditional card game.  Doubtless because of fond childhood memories.

[Rating: 5/10] Played the "setback" variant a lot during my college freshman year ('85-'86, that dates me!)  Really enjoyed it.
